near_miss.lead: Kinship enumerations and father/mother or brother/sister pairs
near_miss.why_not: The Norse legal lists calculate specific inheritance degrees; Vedic charms personify disease or address family, and Russian prose laments loss of compassion. Shared kin terms do not reproduce distinctive syntax or ordering.

near_miss.lead: Marriage and natal family: father, mother, brother, household
near_miss.why_not: Norse consent, guardianship and inheritance provisions overlap with the Vedic curse on a bride only in predictable relatives. There is no stable verbal equation or shared legal formula.
The apparent house term in the Norse pivot is actually ship construction, gerð. Ship financing is not the Vedic prosperity enumeration.
Norse explicitly invokes the Christian Trinity. The Vedic breath/father simile supplies no inherited syntactic counterpart; the Christian wording has a direct historical explanation.

Root-pair corpus search found numerous ordinary Norse lodging statements. Russian lying at night shares cognate lying and night, but Homer uses another verb; the temporal adjunct is too ordinary to establish inheritance.

The AVP kin-killer list and Norse penal clause share a taboo and kin vocabulary, but Norse drepa is not cognate with han. A mother/strike-root search also found worm-destruction charms, demonstrating why lexical co-occurrence alone is insufficient. List order and syntax differ.

near_miss.lead: Warm blood; blood and blossoms; flowering wood
near_miss.why_not: The Sanskrit warrior simile explicitly compares bloodied appearance to a flowering tree; Norse simply reports warm blood entering the sea. The Irish flowering-tree partners belong to the same branch. Warm blood has an external Homeric partner recorded separately.
The second Norse text is a same-branch saint narrative; the Russian excerpt is editorial prose. No cross-branch inherited formula is supported.

near_miss.lead: Neither in life nor death: loyal companions remain together
near_miss.why_not: A conventional totalizing opposition in a late Christian royal narrative; none of the supplied partners shares it. A Greek form search produced incidental living/death vocabulary, no tested phrase-level counterpart.

Norse bæri nafn and Greek οὔνομα φέρεσθαι share cognate object and verb, but one concerns rank and the other the deserved designation of a fortunate life. Name/bear-root search also returns ordinary naming, including Christian glosses. This widespread productive metaphor lacks distinctive inherited elaboration.

near_miss.lead: Tongue articulates words / speech comes from the tongue
near_miss.why_not: Cognate tongue and word occur, but Norse contrasts a poet’s spontaneous verse with halting ordinary speech; Lucretius gives a physiological account. The words do not have the same syntactic relation. Wider tongue/word hits include ordinary and Christian descriptions of speech.

Old English raven search found battlefield scavenger language, but also dawn, Genesis, a personal name and corrupt OCR. This may be Germanic poetic convention; no cross-branch partner was established, and the Sanskrit partners concern food ethics rather than carrion.

Norse kné and svefn correspond lexically to Hittite genu- and šuppariya-. Both describe sleep on another’s lap and subsequent awakening, but Norse separately places the head and says sleep came upon the king; Hittite describes the deity’s sweet sleep with Tešimi. Search found another literal Norse lap-sleep scene and unrelated Greek bent-knee/sleep statements. The natural posture and differing construction do not establish inherited wording. Homer’s living knees and Vedic dream genealogy do not improve the equation.

Norse describes sequential travel during named seasons; the Vedic passages enumerate seasons in blessing. The order is calendrically predictable, and no distinctive shared predicate or figure survives.

Norse positive sleeping after exertion differs from Homer’s repeated sleepless nights and Greek nocturnal plotting. Cognate sleep/night material does not overcome the opposed assertions and ordinary temporal syntax.

search_lead.cognate: Norse varmt (varmr) and Greek θερμόν continue *gwher-; blóð and αἷμα are lexical replacements, not cognates.
search_lead.argument: The Norse battle verse uses bloð with varmt as blood enters the sea; Homer describes still-warm blood emerging from a wound. Both use a warmth adjective with blood and a motion predicate in combat. This is a search lead only: blood’s literal temperature makes independent expression plausible, and the predicates are not cognate.
